title.en: The Courtyard Full of Boots: Lieh Tzŭ's Relapse (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 列子反齊，門庭充盈（莊子）

region.en: The road to Ch'i and back (symbolic pin: Linzi, Shandong, China)
region.zh: 適齊之道（象徵定位：山東臨淄）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Lieh Tzŭ turns back halfway to Ch'i in fear, for five out of ten restaurants would take no payment — conquer men's hearts by force of the external and trouble follows. Later his courtyard is filled with visitors' boots; the Master Poh Hun Wu Jen stands facing the north, cheek wrinkled on his staff, then departs without a word, crying: It is all over! Exerting influence unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn.
summary.zh: 列子行食於十家，五家先逆——驚恐而返。居於鄙，人舍者將見之——見其客而歎曰：戶庭之閒，其人弗睹也！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: When Lieh Tzŭ went to Ch'i, half way there he turned round and came back. Falling in with Poh Hun Wu Jen, the latter said, "How is it you are so soon back again?" "I was afraid," replied Lieh Tzŭ. "Out of ten restaurants at which I ate," said Lieh Tzŭ, "five would take no payment. ... A restaurant keeper is one who lives by retailing soup. When his returns are counted up, his profit is but small, and his influence is next to nothing. But if such a man could act thus, how much more the ruler of a large State? ... That is what I was afraid of."

Shortly afterwards Poh Hun Wu Jen went to visit Lieh Tzŭ, and lo! his court-yard was filled with boots. Poh Hun Wu Jen stood there awhile, facing the north, his cheek all wrinkled by resting it on his staff. Then, without a word, he departed. Upon this being announced to Lieh Tzŭ, he seized his shoes and ran out barefoot. When he reached the outer gate, he called aloud, "Master! now that you have come, will you not give me medicine?" "It is all over!" cried Poh Hun Wu Jen. "I told you that the world would gather around you. It is not that you can make people gather around you. You cannot prevent them from doing so. Of what use would my instruction be? Exerting influence thus unduly over others, you are by them influenced in turn. You disturb your natural constitution, and are of no further account.

title.en: Huan's Suicide and the Dream of the Autumn Pine (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地（莊子）

region.en: Ch'iu-shih, in the Chêng State (Zhengzhou, Henan, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Huan of Chêng graduates as a Confucianist in three years and sends his younger brother to study as a Mihist; when the father takes the Mihist's side, Huan commits suicide — and appears in a dream: It was I who caused your son to become a Mihist. Why give all the credit to him who is but as the fruit of an autumn pine? Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is.
summary.zh: 鄭人緩也呻吟裘氏之地，祗三年而緩為儒；其父以為墨者。緩於十年自殺；其父夢之曰：使而子為墨者，予也——秋柏之實者。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: There was a man of the Chêng State, named Huan. He pursued his studies at a place called Ch'iu-shih. After three years only, he had graduated as a Confucianist; and like a river which fertilises its banks to a distance of nine li, so did his good influence reach into three families. He caused his younger brother to graduate as a Mihist. But inasmuch as in the question of Confucianism versus Mihism, the father took the side of the Mihist, at the end of ten years Huan committed suicide.

Then the father dreamed that Huan appeared to him and said, "It was I who caused your son to become a Mihist. Why give all the credit to him who is but as the fruit of an autumn pine?" Verily God does not reward man for what he does, but for what he is. ... Whereas a man who should regard his distinctive abilities as of his own making, without reference to his parents, would be like the man of Ch'i who dug a well and then wanted to keep others away from it.

title.en: Chu P'ing Man Learns to Slay Dragons (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益（莊子）

region.en: The school of Chih Li I (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 支離益之門（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Chu P'ing Man spends a large patrimony learning under Chih Li I how to kill dragons. By the end of three years he is perfect — but there is no direction in which he can show his skill. TAO cannot be put into practice.
summary.zh: 朱泙漫學屠龍於支離益，單千金之家；三年技成，而無所用其巧。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the dragon-slaying vanity is proverbial. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Chu P'ing Man spent a large patrimony in learning under Chih Li I how to kill dragons. By the end of three years he was perfect, but there was no direction in which he could show his skill. The true Sage regards certainties as uncertainties; therefore he is never up in arms.

title.en: Ts'ao Shang's Hundred Carriages and the Licker of Piles (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 曹商得車，舐痔之譏（莊子）

region.en: The court of Ch'in (Xianyang, Shaanxi, China)

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Ts'ao Shang, the Sung envoy, returns from Ch'in with a hundred carriages and taunts the sandal-making Chuang Tzŭ. The physician who opens a boil gets one carriage; the man who licks his piles gets five — the more degrading the work, the greater the number of carriages. You, Sir, must have been attending to his piles to get so many carriages. Begone with you!
summary.zh: 宋人有曹商者，為宋王使秦；其往也，得車數乘；秦王有疾，舐痔者得車五乘——所治愈下，得車愈多。子豈治其痔邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing). Included as a comparative text — a scholarly framing, not a claim about religious truth.

passages.text: A man of the Sung State, named Ts'ao Shang, acted as political agent for the prince of Sung at the court of the Ch'in State. When he went thither, he had a few carriages; but the prince of Ch'in was so pleased with him that he added one hundred more. On his return to Sung, he visited Chuang Tzŭ and said, "As for living in poverty in a dirty hovel, earning a scanty subsistence by making sandals, with shrivelled face and yellow ears,--this I could not do. Interviewing a powerful ruler, with a retinue of a hundred carriages,--that is my forte."

"When the prince of Ch'in is sick," replied Chuang Tzŭ, "and he summons his physician to open a boil or cleanse an ulcer, the latter gets one carriage. The man who licks his piles gets five. The more degrading the work, the greater the number of carriages given. You, Sir, must have been attending to his piles to get so many carriages. Begone with you!"

title.en: The Pearl Under the Sleeping Dragon's Nose (Zhuangzi)

region.en: Ho-Shang, the riverside hamlet (symbolic pin: Zhenjiang, Jiangsu, China)
region.zh: 河上之家（象徵定位：江蘇鎮江）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: A man presented with ten chariots by the prince of Sung puts on airs before Chuang Tzŭ, who tells of the poor plaiter of rushes whose son dived into the river and got a pearl worth a thousand ounces — from under the nose of the dragon, which must have been asleep. The prince of Sung is fiercer than a dragon: to get these chariots you must have caught him asleep, and when he wakes you will be ground to powder.
summary.zh: 河上有家貧恃緯蕭而食者；其子沒於淵，得千金之珠——必在九重之淵而驪龍頷下，子能得珠者，必遭其睡也。

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the black dragon's pearl became a classic image of perilous gain. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: A man who had been to see the prince of Sung and had been presented with ten chariots, was putting on airs in the presence of Chuang Tzŭ. "At Ho-Shang," said the latter, "there was a poor man who supported his family by plaiting rushes. One day his son dived into the river and got a pearl worth a thousand ounces of silver. The father bade him fetch a stone and smash it to pieces, explaining that he could only have got such a pearl very deep down from under the nose of the dragon, which must have been asleep. And he said he was afraid that when the dragon waked, the boy would have a poor chance.

"Now the State of Sung is deeper than a deep river, and the prince of Sung is fiercer than a dragon. To get these chariots, you must have caught him asleep. And when he wakes, you will be ground to powder."

title.en: The Sacrificial Ox Would Gladly Change Places with a Neglected Calf (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子釣於濮水，龜曳尾；犧牛之喻（莊子）

region.en: Some prince's court (symbolic pin: Song, Henan, China)
region.zh: 聘使之廷（象徵定位：宋，今河南）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: Invited to enter a prince's service, Chuang Tzŭ replies to the envoy: Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox? It is bedecked with ribbons and fares sumptuously — but when it comes to be slaughtered for the temple, would it not gladly exchange places with some neglected calf?
summary.zh: 或聘於莊子；莊子應其使曰：子見夫犧牛乎？衣以文繡，食以芻菽——及其牽而入於太廟，雖欲為孤犢，其可得乎！

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); quoted by Sima Qian in his biographical notice of Zhuangzi. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: Some prince having invited Chuang Tzŭ to enter his service, Chuang Tzŭ said in reply to the envoy, "Sir, have you ever noticed a sacrificial ox? It is bedecked with ribbons and fares sumptuously. But when it comes to be slaughtered for the temple, would it not gladly exchange places with some neglected calf?"

title.en: Heaven and Earth for My Coffin: Chuang Tzŭ's Death-Bed (Zhuangzi)
title.zh: 莊子將死，以天地為棺槨（莊子）

region.en: The death-bed in Sung (Shangqiu, Henan, China)
region.zh: 宋之病榻（象徵定位：河南商丘）

texts.period: Zhuangzi ch. 32, c. 4th-3rd c. BCE (trans. Giles, 1889)

source.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, trans. Herbert A. Giles, ch. 32

summary.en: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples wished to give him a splendid funeral. With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave, are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand? And when they fear the carrion kite: above ground I shall be food for kites; below I shall be food for mole-crickets and ants — why rob one to feed the other?
summary.zh: 莊子將死，弟子欲厚葬之。莊子曰：吾以天地為棺槨，以日月為連璧，星辰為珠璣，萬物為齎送——吾葬具豈不備邪？

sensitivity.note: Canonical text of the Taoist canon (Nanhua zhenjing); the classic statement of the cosmic funeral. Included as a comparative text.

passages.text: When Chuang Tzŭ was about to die, his disciples expressed a wish to give him a splendid funeral. But Chuang Tzŭ said, "With Heaven and Earth for my coffin and shell; with the sun, moon, and stars as my burial regalia; and with all creation to escort me to the grave,--are not my funeral paraphernalia ready to hand?"

"We fear," argued the disciples, "lest the carrion kite should eat the body of our Master"; to which Chuang Tzŭ replied, "Above ground I shall be food for kites; below I shall be food for mole-crickets and ants. Why rob one to feed the other? ... Those who trust to their senses become slaves to objective existences. Those alone who are guided by their intuitions find the true standard."
